A.explanation: N is a unit of force, so $\text{N m}^{-3}$ is weight per unit volume, not mass per unit volume.

B.explanation: $\text{g}$ is mass but $\text{mm}^{-1}$ is 1 divided by length, not by volume, so it cannot be density.

C.explanation: $\text{kg}$ is mass but $\text{cm}^{-2}$ is 1 divided by area, not by volume, so it cannot be density.

D.explanation: $\mu\text{g}$ is a unit of mass and $\text{mm}^{-3}$ is 1 divided by volume, giving mass per unit volume.

hints: Recall the defining equation for density, $\rho = m/V$, so its unit must be a mass unit divided by a volume unit.
Check the power of the length unit in each option - volume needs length to the power 3, so look for $\text{m}^{-3}$, $\text{mm}^{-3}$ or similar.
Check the numerator too - density needs mass such as $\text{kg}$, $\text{g}$ or $\mu\text{g}$, not force such as $\text{N}$.
walkthrough: State the rule: density $= \text{mass} / \text{volume}$, so any unit for density must have the form $\text{mass unit} / \text{length}^3$.
In SI base form this is $\text{kg m}^{-3}$, but any prefixed mass unit over any prefixed cubed length unit is also valid.
Option A uses $\text{N}$, and since $1 \text{ N} = 1 \text{ kg m s}^{-2}$ it is force per volume, which is weight density, not mass density.
Options B and C use mass numerators $\text{g}$ and $\text{kg}$ but denominators $\text{mm}^{-1}$ and $\text{cm}^{-2}$, which are 1/length and 1/area, not 1/volume.
Option D uses mass $\mu\text{g}$ divided by volume in $\text{mm}^3$, written as $\mu\text{g mm}^{-3}$, which matches mass per unit volume.
Therefore only the $\mu\text{g mm}^{-3}$ combination has the correct mass over length-cubed structure. This is option D.
